title: Chapter 167 – Seven at the Table
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Lin Jian, the child]

The boy has a room, and nobody else knows about it.

It is a small round room with a stove in the corner and a window that looks out on a valley he has only ever seen from the inside of someone else's eyes. The stove is warm. The floor is made of boards. There is a rag rug in front of the fire, and a little stool, and a shelf with seven stones on it, each of them smooth and a different color. He found the stones one by one, over a hundred and nineteen years, in the places where his brother's heart went quiet. He keeps them where he can see them.

He is sitting on the rug now, with his knees drawn up, listening to Jian sleep.

It is a good sound. It is the slow, uneven, rattling sound of an old man's breath, and the boy has learned to count the catches in it the way Bell counts a pulse. Eleven since midnight. Nine in the hour before dawn. The wax pills Bell makes him swallow have eased the worst of it, and the cough has not come back for three days. But the boy has been awake the whole time, in the small round room, listening for the tenth catch. He does not like to leave it unheard.

He knows where each of the stones came from.

The gray one is from the night his father was buried, the first night the voice in his head was loud enough to hear. The blue one is from the day Wuping died, a flat river pebble he found in his brother's hand without knowing how it got there. The red is the color of Yue's cloak the first time she smiled. The pale one, almost white, he does not like to look at. It is from the Gate. He keeps it on the top shelf, in the corner, and does not touch it.

Seven stones. Seven things he could not bear to forget.

He wonders sometimes what the eighth would be.

Are you awake? says a voice.

It is not his brother's. It is thin and bright and amused, and it comes from somewhere above the window, as if a bird had spoken.

Mei? he says. He gets to his feet. He is not used to being spoken to here.

Hello, little one. A small laugh. I wondered whether you could hear me. Papa says the eighth cot does something to the seal. It makes a door.

A door?

Between your room and the Annex. The voice is warm and a little shy. I thought you might like to sit at the table.

* * *

He does not understand it at first.

He has been in his brother's mind for as long as he can remember, and the only table he has ever had is the one in the old house at home, the one his mother scrubbed on Wednesdays, which he can see only through memory. But Mei tells him, in her thread of a voice, that the eighth bed was built to carry two. One for the body. One for the one who lives inside. That a child with a seal can step out of his room if the door is open, and sit at a table, and be seen, for as long as the cot's lamp burns.

It costs, she says. Everything does. A little of me, and a little of him. But Papa did the sum, and it's small.

Will it hurt Brother?

He'll be asleep. It's the only way. A pause. Do you want to?

The boy looks at the stove, and the stones, and the window. He thinks of the seven small children in the Annex, and Ao's hand on the rabbit, and Tao's top. He thinks of how many times he has wanted to say hello to them, and has only ever had a whisper.

Yes, he says.

Something in the room changes. The window goes bright. The door, which he has never noticed before, appears in the wall beside the stove, a plain wooden door with a latch, and light comes under it in a thin gold line.

He puts his hand on the latch.

Don't be scared, says Mei.

I'm not.

Good. She sounds as if she is smiling. Neither am I.

* * *

The Annex is warm, and it is full of faces, and every one of them is looking at him.

He stands in the middle of the floor, in the lamplight, in his bare feet. He is wearing a plain white smock. His hands are small. They are the hands of a boy of about eight, with scabbed knuckles and a bitten thumb, and he is staring down at them as though they were a gift.

He can feel the floor. It is cold and rough. He can feel the warmth of the stove on his left side and the draft from the door on his right. He can smell apples.

"Hello," he says.

His voice is high and clear and cracked at the edges. It is nothing like Jian's. It is his own.

For a long moment, nobody breathes.

Then Ao, who is sitting on a stool with the rabbit in his lap, says in a hushed and wondering voice, "He's little."

"I'm eight," the boy says, a bit defensively.

"I'm three." Ao considers this. "Are you a ghost?"

"No." The boy thinks. "I'm Brother's... I'm the one inside."

"Oh!" Ao's face lights. "You're the blue."

"I suppose."

"I like you!" says Ao, with total finality, and slides off the stool and runs across the floor and seizes him round the waist with both arms. The boy staggers. He does not know what to do with his hands. He puts them, tentatively, on the small shaggy head, and it is warm, and it smells of rice and soap, and he feels something in his chest give way, like a seam.

Oh, he thinks. This is what it is.

Behind Ao, Tao is scowling. "He's skinny," he says.

"So are you," says Mo Yan, in a silver whisper that is not a voice. The boy hears it clearly, a thin cracked bell in the back of his head. He looks across the room. The girl with the charcoal is looking at him gravely, and she lifts her hand, and waves.

* * *

After Ao, they come to him one at a time.

Duan Ke is first. He stands in front of the boy with his arms folded and his jaw set, as though about to deliver a verdict, and looks him up and down for a full ten seconds. Then he says, very gruffly, "You look like a kid who could use a sword lesson."

"I'm eight."

"Exactly." He draws the pale blade a hand's breadth from the scabbard and slides it back. "Tomorrow, after the dawn drill. Don't be late."

The boy nods, dazed. Duan Ke gives a short, awkward jerk of the head, and goes away quickly, and Cheng Hui, behind him, looks up from his leather book and says dryly, "He likes you."

"How can you tell?"

"He has not told you to get lost."

Hai Ren is next. The monk does not speak. He bows, a slow, precise, formal bow, with his long hands folded, and the boy, not knowing what else to do, bows back. When they straighten, Hai Ren is smiling, and it is a very small smile, but it changes the shape of his whole face.

"I have listened to you for a long time," the monk says softly. "Through the old man. It is good to hear you with my ears."

Zhen Li comes last, with his lamp. He holds it out in both hands without a word. The boy takes it. It is warm, and heavier than it looks, and the little flame inside it leans toward him like a cat.

"It likes you," says Zhen Li, wonderingly. "It doesn't like anyone."

"I don't know why."

"Neither do I." The tired gray eyes are bright. "But I've forgotten a lot of things. Maybe I knew."

* * *

Nurse has set a table in the middle of the Annex.

It is a plain round table of pale wood, with eight stools drawn up to it and a ninth chair at the head. The ninth has a cushion on it. On the table are nine cups of tea, each one filled to the brim, and a plate of small rice cakes that she must have steamed in the dark. Nurse stands behind the empty ninth chair with her hands folded, and her face is wet.

"I thought you ought to have a proper meal," she says. "All of you. Together. For once."

The boy looks at the table. He counts the stools. Ao and Tao on one side. Mo Yan, Zhen Li, Hai Ren, Duan Ke, Cheng Hui in a half circle. The eighth stool is for him. Next to it, a little apart, is an empty bowl of water.

"What's that for?"

For me, says Mei, from the grille in the wall. Papa asked Nurse to set it. So that I'd have a place.

The boy sits.

The stool is hard, and a little too high, and it wobbles. He grips the edge of the table and looks round at the faces, one after another, at Duan Ke's stern broken nose and Cheng Hui's elegant frown, at Hai Ren's dark eyes and Zhen Li's tired smile. These are his brothers and sisters. He has been in the same house with them for fifty days. He has never before been able to say their names to their faces.

"Hello," he says again. "I'm Lin Jian. I'm the eighth."

"We know," says Cheng Hui, gently. "We are glad to see you at last."

"Is everyone here?"

"Everyone but the old man," says Duan Ke. "He's asleep. Bell said not to wake him."

"Good." The boy takes a breath. "Then this is a council. And it's... a hard one."

He looks round the table. Seven faces look back.

"Mr. Cole wants to tell us what the Nine are," he says.

* * *

Ethan tells it from the grille, in the thin, cracked, unhurried voice of a man reading from a page he has written on his own heart.

There were nine of us who raised the Hall, he says. Nine families. Nine cohorts. We were not kings, nor priests, nor soldiers. We were what remained of a world that was ending. Every one of us had a reason to build a place where the dying could sleep.

The room is silent. The boy sits with his hands in his lap, and the tea steams.

We did not call ourselves the Nine at first. It was only that when we met, there were nine chairs, and each of us took one. I took the ninth. I was the youngest. I had no gift but arithmetic and a daughter who was ill. A faint, dry laugh. The others had gifts that I envied. A woman who could hold a mountain still. A man who could sing a fever down. A boy not much older than you, Lin Jian, who could dream the future and was never wrong.

We swore a vow. The vow is on the stone. That none should be woken from the Hall's sleep except by the consent of all nine. We swore it because we were afraid that one of us, in grief or greed or desperation, would try to use the sleepers. We did not trust ourselves. He pauses. We were right not to.

"What happened?" Cheng Hui asks.

The other eight died. The voice is flat. Some in the first century, some in the third. Two in the war that ended the world above. One by his own hand. One by mine.

Ao's head comes up.

I will tell you that story, says Ethan, but not today. I have told you the only part that matters now. The Nine are dead, except for me. And a vow needs nine hands. He draws a breath. I scratched the ninth circle on the stone, because I could not bear to look at it. I was the last one left. I was the one who broke the vow. And I think, children, that I have been waiting six hundred years for nine new hands.

* * *

The boy's mouth is dry.

He looks at the teacup, and the steam rising off it, and the plate of rice cakes. Then he looks at Cheng Hui, whose face has gone still as a mask.

"You want us to be the Nine," says the scholar.

I do.

"The eight Operators. And Mei."

Yes. The voice cracks. It is not an accident. I made the eight of you so that, when the time came, there would be eight voices that I trusted. And one that I loved.

Duan Ke's hand has found his sword. "And what do you want us to consent to?"

A choice. Ethan's words come very slowly. The Hall has a reserve. Not a great one. At the bottom of the dome there are twelve thousand sleepers whom the Nine set apart. Wardens, we called them. They were chosen for strength, and trained for it, and they were meant to wake if the Hall was ever attacked. Cultivators. Soldiers. People who could hold a Wall.

"Twelve thousand," says Duan Ke softly.

If you consent to wake them, they will wake. All twelve thousand. It will take three days. His voice shakes. And it will take everything the Gate has left.

The boy feels the cold go down his spine. "Everything."

Mei. The word is a whisper. She will not survive it.

* * *

Nobody speaks. The stove ticks. One of the lamps gutters, and Zhen Li, without looking, lifts a finger, and it steadies.

"No," says Tao.

He says it loudly, defiantly, with his small fist clenched on the table. "No. We're not doing that. She's Mei."

"I agree," says Hai Ren, calmly.

"And I," says Zhen Li.

Ao has begun to cry, silently, with his face pressed into the rabbit. Mo Yan has taken up her charcoal. On the table, among the teacups, she draws a girl with a crown of light, and around the girl a ring of twelve thousand small stick figures, all of them holding hands, and over the whole of it a very large, very black X.

No, she says, in the back of the boy's head, in her cracked silver way.

Cheng Hui lets out a breath. "It is unanimous, then?"

"It is not," says Duan Ke.

All eyes turn to him. The sword boy has gone pale. His jaw is set hard, and his hand is white on the hilt.

"I don't want to vote for it," he says. "I want that said. But the Wall needs soldiers. We've got seven children and a broken old man. If there's twelve thousand men who can fight, and the price is one girl, I—" He stops. He closes his eyes. "I don't know how to say it. I hate that I'm thinking it."

"You are thinking it," says Cheng Hui quietly, "because you are good at war."

"That's not a compliment."

"No."

The room is very still.

It's all right, Duan Ke, says Mei. Her voice comes from the wall, bright and thin. You can say it. I'd rather you did. If you don't, you'll think it all night.

The sword boy covers his face with his hand.

* * *

Mei speaks to him alone while the others argue by the stove.

You're quiet, she says, softly.

I'm thinking.

About the Wardens?

About you. He looks at the bowl of water beside his stool, and the faint ripple on its surface that must be her. Everyone said no so fast. Tao nearly shouted. But I don't think it's fair, that nobody asked you.

Oh. A small, surprised laugh. Well. I would say no, too.

Why?

Because I've seen what they cost. Her voice is gentle. Twelve thousand people, woken into a world that has lost everything they knew. And I would be the thing that woke them. I'd rather be a girl in a well than a reason.

He bites his lip.

But I want you to know I wasn't afraid of it, she says. I want that said. If it came to a choice, I wouldn't have hated you for making it. A pause. You're allowed to choose what's hard. That's all I wanted to tell you.

I don't want to choose.

I know. Her voice drops to a whisper. That's why you're good at it.

* * *

Duan Ke leaves the table, afterward, and the boy goes after him.

He finds the sword boy at the end of the corridor, with his forehead pressed to the cold plaster and his fists clenched at his sides. His back is shaking. He does not turn when the boy stops behind him, but he says, in a muffled, furious voice, "Go away."

"No."

"I mean it. I don't want to be looked at."

"You can face the wall." The boy sits down on the floor with his back against the opposite side of the corridor and folds his legs. "I'll look at the floor. We can both not look at each other."

A long silence. Then a sound that might be a laugh, or might be the opposite.

"I was going to say yes," Duan Ke says, thickly. "To the twelve thousand. I was going to vote yes, and watch her go."

"I know."

"What kind of person does that?"

"A soldier," says the boy.

"That's not an answer."

"It's the only one I have." He picks at the scab on his knuckle. "Brother says that when he was young, he used to think the worst thing a person could be was weak. And then he learned that the worst thing was to be strong in the wrong direction."

Duan Ke slides slowly down the wall until he is sitting too. He wipes his face with his sleeve.

"I'm sixteen," he says. "I'm not supposed to know this stuff."

"None of us are," says the boy.

They sit in the corridor for a long time, not looking at each other, and the lamps burn.

* * *

It is Cheng Hui who frames the second question.

He does it with a clearness that is almost unbearable, laying out the terms on the back of a sheet of paper with his fine pen. If the Wardens are not woken, there are two paths. They can stay in the Hall and hold it as long as they can. Or they can leave, all seven of them, with the eighth, and carry what they have to the valley and the Wall.

"What happens if we leave?" Ao asks.

"We think our patterns fade." Cheng Hui's voice is gentle. "Not at once. Perhaps in a year. Perhaps less. The beds were tuned to us, and without them we have only what Jian carries."

"And if we stay?"

"Then the Hall holds until the third wave, and perhaps a few waves more, and then it does not." He taps the paper. "I cannot tell you which is better. I can only tell you what each costs."

"I'll stay," says Tao, at once.

"I'll stay with Tao," says Ao.

"I cannot leave the lamps," says Zhen Li. He says it simply, with his brass lantern in his lap. "If I go, they go out. It's two hundred, or a hundred and fifty. I don't know. But they would go out."

Hai Ren bows his head. "I will go. The Hall has need of lamps, not of stillness. I do not wish to choose, but I think the lamps are in better hands than mine."

"I'll go," says Duan Ke. His voice is rough. "If there's a Wall, I belong on it."

"And I," says Cheng Hui. "Though I would prefer to leave a word behind."

Mo Yan draws a question mark and holds it up.

The boy looks at the paper. He looks at the faces. He is the youngest of them in one way and the oldest in another, and he does not know what to do.

"That's three," he says slowly. "Three and three. And Mo Yan doesn't know."

And I can't vote, says Mei, from the wall. I wouldn't know how. It's Papa's choice, in a way, and mine, and I don't want to be the reason.

Cheng Hui looks round the table. "Then we are tied."

"Tied," says Tao, glaring.

"Which leaves the eighth."

The boy's stomach drops.

* * *

He did not know he would have to.

He sits on the wobbling stool and looks at his own small hands, at the scabbed knuckles, at the bitten thumb. He hears the stove, and the lamps, and the tap of Cheng Hui's pen. He hears, a long way off, in the small round room behind the door, his brother's breath catching on the tenth beat.

Brother, he thinks. Are you there?

Always. The old voice is a whisper, faint with sleep. I am sorry. I cannot be at the table. But I am here.

They want me to choose.

I know. A pause. I will not choose for you. It is your life, and theirs, and I would not take it from you.

What would you do?

It does not matter.

It matters to me.

A long silence. Then, very slowly, the voice says, I would go. I would carry them to my mother, and the tree, and the Wall. I would do it because I believe that people ought to be with the ones who love them when they have little time left. And because I am a coward, and cannot bear to watch the Hall fall. A breath. But I have lived a long time, and I have been wrong often.

The boy closes his eyes.

He thinks of the valley. He thinks of his mother's hands on the bowl, and the black bark of the tree, and the shape of the Wall against the stars. He thinks of Ao's face when he first saw a stuffed rabbit mended eleven times, and of the thirty-one names in the book, and the forty-one that were rested.

He thinks: They have had so little time.

And he opens his eyes, and he says, in a voice that surprises him with how steady it is, "We go."

"Brother—" Tao begins.

"We go," says the boy. "All of us. We take the seven, and we go to the valley, and we fight where the fight is. And we come back." He looks at Zhen Li. "Not to stay. To visit. As long as there's a Hall to come back to."

"And the lamps?" says Zhen Li.

"We teach someone else." He looks at Nurse. "If she'll let us."

Nurse's hands tighten on the chair. Her mouth trembles. "I have kept lamps for six hundred years," she says. "I can keep a hundred and nineteen."

The boy nods. His throat hurts. Somewhere behind the door in his mind there is a small sound, like a pebble set down on a shelf, and he knows without looking that the eighth stone has arrived. He looks down at the table, at the nine cups of tea, one of them untouched.

"It's a hard thing," he says. "I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. But I think it's right."

Tao says nothing. His small face is red. He is clutching his top so tightly that his knuckles shine.

Then, quite slowly, he reaches across the table and pushes the plate of rice cakes toward the boy.

"Eat," he says gruffly. "You're skinny."
